  relationship_status: Widowed

  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Kai was sixty-five when the quiet in his house finally grew too heavy to carry alone. Five years prior, his youngest daughter’s sudden collapse had begun in their driveway, a swift transition from laughter to the sharp, metallic tang of antiseptic and the staccato rhythm of monitors. He remembered the exact second the emergency responders arrived, their hands moving with urgent certainty while his own palms remained slick against his thighs. He had tried to explain her condition, his voice fracturing over the word nebulizer, but the pause between his directions and their first intervention had stretched into an eternity. When they wheeled her past him toward the trauma bay, the heavy doors closing behind the gurney felt absolute. He was certain that the minutes lost in the waiting room were the minutes she had almost lost forever. In the months that followed, Kai’s routines shifted. He stopped answering his landline, bracing for the shrill ring that might spell emergency, and began taking circuitous routes to avoid ambulance lights reflecting off wet pavement. When his own shoulders grew tight and his breathing turned shallow after raking the yard, he found himself gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened, his chest tightening with a sudden, suffocating panic. What frightened him most was the way his body remembered the trauma bay before his mind could catch up. He tried hard not to think about the sterile corridors, the beeping monitors, the look on the attending physician’s face. When the memories surfaced, he immediately turned on the television, opened a spreadsheet, or called his sister to discuss grocery lists, filling every quiet hour until his thoughts had no room to wander backward. Now, as a project manager overseeing facility renovations across three counties, Kai navigated a landscape that felt increasingly hostile. He had come to believe the collapse happened because of the way he acted that first day, that his hesitation at the curb had cost his daughter her rhythm. The appraisal sat heavy in his chest alongside a persistent self-doubt that made every delegation feel like a gamble he was destined to lose. At work, he avoided the building’s occupational health clinic, telling his executive assistant that his personal physician preferred to handle his annual physical. He could not tolerate the thought of undergoing a medical examination, of lying back in a paper-covered chair while a stranger listened to his heart, knowing the sight of the cuff inflating would bring a violent surge of anger and shame. When project updates were delayed past the agreed deadline, Kai’s stomach would drop, and he would immediately begin drafting contingency plans, assuming the delay meant a hidden disaster was unfolding. His colleagues noticed the change. He stopped attending site visits where contractors discussed safety protocols, citing scheduling conflicts, and his reliability at the firm began to fracture under the weight of his own withdrawals. The breaking point arrived when his primary care physician, frustrated by his repeated cancellations, mandated a telehealth visit. Kai sat in his study, staring at the darkened monitor, his breath coming in short, sharp pulls. He was tired of the exhausting architecture of his avoidance, tired of the way the past had colonized his present. He had come to believe he should have protected her, and the failure echoed in every quiet moment of his widowed life. He picked up the phone to schedule an in-person appointment, hoping the clinician might help him untangle the knot between his own breathing and the ghost of a child’s first breath. He was afraid the fear would never leave him, but he was desperate to stop running from the places where life, finally, was just living.
